thread.title: How To Retire In Your 60s Without Going Broke

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: How To Retire In Your 60s Without Going Broke
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Investors hunting for solid dividend stocks should emphasize dividend growers. Several of the dividend growers carry risk ratings of 2.5 or below. Reference for my risk ratings:
This is a great starting point for investors focusing on a long-term portfolio that should grow dividends faster than inflation.
The Problem Many retirees face a problem when it comes to picking a strategy to construct their portfolio. In short, not all strategies are created equal. One of the more depressing strategies to hear about is investors demanding an overall yield of around 14%. This is an unreasonable goal and an easy way to enter retirement without enjoying an actual retirement.
The prolonged bull market brings up a major problem when investors are only focusing on the short term. Unreasonable returns seem reasonable if we’re just looking at the recent bull market. When it comes to investing over several decades, a 14% yield is a quick way to go broke.
Investors using this strategy may be tempted to “diversify” their portfolio by investing in several high dividend yield stocks. This results in having a portfolio filled with significantly risky investments. “Diversifying” a large portion of the portfolio in high-yield stocks with very little understanding of the underlying fundamentals is a bad idea. Instead, investors should be looking to build a well-rounded, diversified portfolio.
The solution Investors who don’t enjoy researching a significant number of companies should look to ETFs or companies that have a proven track record. From what I’ve seen, it’s rare to see a sucker yield from large companies with a strong track record. Here are some stocks that would make a great start to a diversified portfolio:

Retirees should look at diversifying across several sectors. ETFs are also an option, such as the Vanguard Utilities ETF ( VPU ) for utilities, for investors to get an allocation to certain sectors.
Equity REITs are excellent for investors or retirees seeking higher yields.
For investors interested in real estate, see my guide on investing in real estate .
Do you like real estate?
Most investors do.
Real estate is the most popular investment for long-term wealth creation. Many investors don’t realize that investing in equity REITs is very similar to buying physical rental properties. If an investor were to buy out an entire REIT, they would directly own all of the real estate. Most investors only purchase a very small portion of the REIT’s equity. However, the return they are earning should still reflect the performance of the real estate over the long term.
A REIT is far better than buying real estate directly Real estate is a great investment for building wealth. The 3 biggest barriers to investing in real estate are:
The high transactions costs.
Enormous minimum amount to invest.
Difficulty of managing your own rental property.
What makes REITs better?
If an investor wants to buy a condo in a coastal market, the price tag could easily exceed $300,000. They could get a mortgage to help with the cost, but they would still be expected to come up with $60,000 to $90,000. In several coastal markets, the prices are even higher.
When the investor buys and sells this physical real estate, they will need a realtor. Between the costs of hiring the realtor and paying the related fees and taxes, the investor can lose a significant chunk of their investment. In some cases, it is near 10%.
A REIT allows the investor to have dramatically lower expenses. The REIT can be traded with a very small commission. Most brokers will charge less than $10 on the transaction.
By purchasing shares of a REIT instead, the investor can put much smaller amounts of money to work. They can begin building their wealth without spending $300,000 in one single investment.
Do you like repairing air conditioning units or fixing plumbing problems?
I don’t either.
Directly owning a rental property leaves the investor to handle the day-to-day operations. I own several REITs. None of my REITs have ever called to ask me to perform repairs. They have consistently paid dividends to me, but they have not asked me to perform work.
Do you like doing taxes?
I despise tax complications. Owning a REIT is dramatically simpler for taxes than owning a rental property. The REIT keeps records and makes the investors’ tax time a breeze.
Do you like dealing with tenants who are late on paying rent?
I don’t care for that either. The REIT handles it all for you.
They screen the tenants for you.
They select the best tenants for you.
They collect the rent for you
They repair the property for you.
They handle the tax implications for you.
Do you remember the paperwork for your last mortgage? Was that an enjoyable experience?
REITs are better than investing in the property directly because they can handle the bank for you.
In addition to dealing with the bank, the REIT also gets a lower interest rate on their loan than you can get as an individual investor.
A REIT is better than investing directly in real estate because the REIT carries better insurance.
If you purchased that condo for $300,000 and a storm destroyed the property, you would be stuck spending countless hours dealing with the insurance company. They most likely wouldn’t provide any replacement for the revenue lost while the property was rebuilt.
The REITs carry insurance to cover that event. It is already priced in. Even if an asset were destroyed, it would not have a significant negative impact on the REIT. It would not prevent them from continuing to pay your dividend.
REITs are better than buying real estate because they can occasionally be purchased for a significant discount to the value of the real estate. This provides an added source of return for investors.
Investors have the opportunity to purchase some excellent REITs at a discount to the value of the assets. Some weaker REITs also trade at significant discounts. However, there are regularly many great REITs that are on sale if an investor knows where to look.
Excellent REITs I would like to highlight some excellent REITs:
Simon Property Group ( SPG ), AvalonBay ( AVB ), and Equity Lifestyle ( ELS ) have risk ratings of “1.” These REITs know how to manage their balance sheet and their cash flows.
Simon Property Group During Q1, SPG repurchased 1,473,588 shares of stock. There are about 320 million shares issued and outstanding, so that was a nice buyback. We’re not looking for SPG to weaken their balance sheet by being very aggressive on the buyback, just to boost their growth in net asset value per share and FFO per share by repurchasing a little bit. Buying back 1% to 2% per year would be enough to be quite attractive in the current environment.
Their forward guidance does not include the impact of repurchasing any stock. They are currently trading between 13x and 14x forward FFO, so buybacks are quite effective at boosting FFO per share.
On the earnings call, David Simon was quite explicit about retailers accepting returns in store for sales made online. They allow that and are happy to provide the convenience to customers. However, the store is not permitted to modify their “net sales” for the location by deducting the in-store return of an online sale. This is outlined in the leases.
He is very confident that this is happening. Without this behavior, the reported sales per square foot would be higher. Despite this challenge to reported sales per square foot, the value came in at a $641 for the trailing 12 months. That is an increase of 4.2% year over year.
All 3 companies know how to create steady dividend growth with lower risk.
Equity Lifestyle Recently, the dividend growth for ELS has been absurdly high.
Source: ELS investors presentation
Over the last 5 years, they had a 17% compound annual growth rate. ELS is a good REIT. They cannot sustain that growth rate.
They can easily sustain the current dividend level. They can consistently grow that dividend throughout the next decade. However, any investors hoping for a long-term continuation of 17% growth rates has unrealistic expectations.
AvalonBay Apartment REITs will be getting a little extra attention because of the favorable fundamentals for the sector. Several of them have solid balance sheets and steady growth. The demographics are also favorable for apartment REITs. It is ironic to see so many positive factors for a sector where some of the best players are trading at a discount to the rough estimated value of their assets.
Source: AVB investor presentation
The apartment REIT fundamentals are supported by a moderate growth in workers entering the 25 to 34-year-old age bracket. Those potential renters are generally doing well over the last couple of years in the labor market. The increase in the average age for first marriage and beginning motherhood is another positive factor for apartment REITs. It makes the apartment lifestyle more attractive for a longer period during which many of the expected renters should be seeing growth in their wages. This won’t be true for every single individual, but on the broader level, it creates a positive tailwind for apartment REIT performance.
Final thoughts The dividend growth for SPG, AVB, and ELS should materially outpace inflation over the next 20 years. These are great stocks to build a retirement portfolio. They offer reasonable dividend yields up front and substantial dividend growth. SPG, AVB, ELS are all deserving of a buy rating .
